People think I am listening for the number. I am not. I already have the number, it was in the file. What I am listening for is whether you know why it moved. If attrition goes from nine to fourteen and you tell me it went from nine to fourteen, you have told me nothing I did not have on Friday. Tell me it is concentrated in one site, that it started when the shift pattern changed, and that two thirds of the leavers had less than a year of service. Now I can do something. The second thing I listen for is whether you tell me the bad one before I find it. If I find it, I stop trusting the rest of the presentation, and that is not personal, it is arithmetic. And the third thing, honestly, is whether you can say I do not know. Nobody has ever lost credibility with me for saying I do not know and I will have it by Thursday.

My worst presentation had eleven slides and every one of them was true. That was the problem. Eleven true things is not an argument, it is a filing cabinet, and by slide four the room had gone quiet in the way that means nobody is listening. What I do now is decide the sentence before I decide the numbers. One sentence. Last quarter, ours was: we are not losing people to money, we are losing them to their first ninety days. Then every number I brought either supported that sentence or stayed at home. Three charts instead of eleven. And here is the part that surprised me. The questions got harder, not easier, because for the first time people understood what I was claiming and could argue with it. That is what you want. A room that argues with you is a room that heard you.
